1. the model-simulared rainfall, heating and moisture budgets compare well to those diagnosed from soundings, 2. the model results have higher temporal variability, 3. the model underestimates rainfall by 17–20%, and 4. the model-simulation results of the two convective periods are similar, except for the larger CAPE and stronger vertical wind shear during June.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the simulation of two convective periods in the South China Sea using the Goddard cumulus ensemble (GCE) two-dimensional cloud-resolving model.
the simulation of the convective systems that occur over the South China Sea during SCSMEX.
understanding the role of the diurnal cycle in the South China Sea monsoon and its relationship with the large-scale circulation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the GCE model is capable of simulating the observed temporal and spatial variation of rainfall, the time-averaged heating rate and moisture budget, and the diurnal variation of rainfall.
the GCE model has successfully reproduced many of the observed characteristics of the two SCSMEX convective systems.
the model is able to reproduce the major features of the observed convective systems over the South China Sea.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are able to simulate the observed diurnal and synoptic variations of rainfall, heating, and moisture budget over the SCSMEX domain.
the GCE model can be used for simulating the convective systems over the South China Sea.
the two-dimensional GCE model with a semiprognosic forcing scheme can be a useful tool in studying convective systems over the SCS.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have shown that a cloud-resolving model with a semiprognosis approach can be used for simulating convective systems over a relatively large area, in this case over the SCS.

the GCE model is able to simulate the temporal variation of the observed rainfall, time-averaged heating and moisture budgets, and convective system characteristics (e.g., size, intensity, and location) reasonably well.
